sections.b: The book of Haggai has two chapters, four dated messages and 38 verses. On 29 August 520 BC the word comes to the governor Zerubbabel and the high priest Joshua: the people say the time has not come, but they live in finished houses while the Temple is desolate and their harvests fail. They obey, and the work begins on 21 September. On 17 October (the seventh day of Booths) the prophet answers the old people's grief at the new house's size with "Be strong, I am with you" and a promise of a greater last glory. On 18 December the priests rule that holiness does not spread by touch but uncleanness does, the LORD promises "from this day on I will bless," and Zerubbabel is named the LORD's seal ring.

Haggai's four dated messages are the reason the Second Temple was built. The people had stopped (Ezra 4:24); Haggai tells them to go up for wood (1:8), the leaders and the remnant obey, and the work begins on 21 September 520 BC (1:14-15). On the seventh day of Booths he meets the grief of the old people who remember Solomon's Temple with "Be strong, for I am with you" and a promise that the last glory will be greater than the first (2:1-9). The priests' ruling and the turn to blessing on 18 December (2:10-19) tie the people's harvests to the house.
sections.refs: Haggai 1:8; Haggai 1:14-15; Haggai 2:1-9; Haggai 2:15-19; Ezra 5:1-2; Ezra 6:14-15

sections.b: In Haggai the Temple is the test of the community's priorities. The LORD asks the people to build a house he will take pleasure in and in which he will be honored (1:8). He names the house "desolate" in a wordplay with the drought (1:4, 9, 11), and promises to fill it with glory and to give peace in that place (2:7-9). The comparison with Solomon's Temple, "Is it not like nothing in your eyes?" (2:3), is the book's main pastoral problem.

sections.h: In Haggai: governor, builder, seal ring
sections.b: Haggai addresses Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel as governor of Judah (1:1, 14; 2:2, 21), alongside Joshua the high priest. The LORD rouses his spirit (1:14), tells him to be strong (2:4), and on 18 December 520 promises on the day the nations' thrones are overturned to take him as "my servant" and make him "like a seal ring, for I have chosen you" (2:23). The language is David's, and it reverses Jeremiah's word about Zerubbabel's grandfather (Jeremiah 22:24-25). The book never calls him king, and the sources do not say what happened to the promise.

Haggai names Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, with Zerubbabel as the leader of the community. The LORD rouses his spirit with the governor's and the people's (1:14), and he is called to be strong (2:4). Haggai gives him a place in the book's order of leaders, equal to the governor. Ezra calls the same man Jeshua. His father Jehozadak was exiled in 586 BC (1 Chronicles 6:15).
sections.refs: Haggai 1:1; Haggai 1:12; Haggai 1:14; Haggai 2:2; Haggai 2:4; Ezra 3:2; 1 Chronicles 6:15

sections.h: Darius I and the dates of Haggai
sections.b: Haggai dates every message by the regnal year of Darius I, who took the throne in 522 BC and put down revolts in his first two years. The dates fall between 29 August and 18 December 520 BC by the usual conversion, in the province of Judah (Yehud) under a Persian-appointed governor. Haggai's "shaking of the heavens and the earth, the nations" has often been read against those unsettled years (2:6-7, 21-22). The Temple was finished in Darius's sixth year (Ezra 6:15).
sections.refs: Haggai 1:1; Haggai 2:1; Haggai 2:10; Haggai 2:6-7; Haggai 2:21-22; Ezra 6:15

sections.h: "The remnant of the people" in Haggai
sections.b: In Haggai the remnant (she'erit ha'am) is the community of his own day: the returned exiles and the poor farming population of Judah. It is introduced when the leaders and "all the remnant of the people" obey (1:12), is roused with them (1:14), and is addressed with them on the last day of Booths (2:2). Before it listens, the LORD speaks of "this people" (1:2); the change of word is part of the book's argument.

sections.h: The first glory and the last (Haggai)
sections.b: Haggai uses kavod of the house: "Who is left among you who saw this house in its first glory?" (2:3), "I will fill this house with glory" (2:7), and "the last glory of this house will be greater than the first" (2:9). The LORD also says in 1:8 that he will "be honored" by the building, using the verb of the same root. The promise echoes the cloud that filled the tabernacle and Solomon's Temple (Exodus 40:34-35; 1 Kings 8:10-11) and the vision in which the glory returns (Ezekiel 43:1-5). Jewish tradition says the Shekhinah did not fill the Second Temple (Yoma 21b).
sections.refs: Haggai 1:8; Haggai 2:3; Haggai 2:7; Haggai 2:9; Exodus 40:34-35; 1 Kings 8:10-11; Ezekiel 43:1-5

sections.b: On 18 December 520 BC Haggai asks the priests two questions: does holy meat carried in a robe make other food holy, and does a person made unclean by a corpse make food unclean? The priests answer no, then yes. Holiness is not caught by touch from a garment's fold; corpse uncleanness is. Haggai applies it to "this people" and their offerings (2:14). The first answer rests on Leviticus 6:27, the second on Numbers 19:11-22.

sections.h: Failed harvests and "from this day I will bless"
sections.b: Haggai reads the poor harvests of 520 BC as the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28 and Leviticus 26: much sown and little brought in, a bag with holes, the heavens withholding dew, blight, mildew and hail (1:6-11; 2:16-17). On the day the work reaches a milestone the sentence turns: "From this day on I will bless" (2:19). Zechariah 8:9-12 says the same. The book speaks to one community at one moment and is not a rule that giving brings wealth.
sections.refs: Haggai 1:6; Haggai 1:9-11; Haggai 2:16-19; Deuteronomy 28:38-40; Deuteronomy 11:13-17; Leviticus 26:19-20

sections.h: "The word that I cut with you" (Haggai 2:5)
sections.b: Haggai appeals to the Exodus covenant in a shortened phrase: "the word that I cut with you when you came out of Egypt." The Hebrew lacks the usual noun "covenant" after the verb "cut," and the Greek omits the clause. The promise attached to it is that the LORD's spirit "is standing among you," so they should not be afraid. The shaking of the nations (2:6-7) comes after, as the Exodus preceded Sinai.

The last oracle of Haggai uses the holy war picture: the LORD overturns the throne of kingdoms and the chariot, horses and riders go down "each by the sword of his brother." The image is of Gideon's night (Judges 7:22) and Gog's fall (Ezekiel 38:21). The people do not fight. The LORD does the shaking, and the chosen governor is the one on whom the promise rests.

Haggai is among the most exactly dated and most quickly obeyed prophets: the people respond within weeks (1:12-15), and Ezra credits his and Zechariah's prophecy with the Temple's completion (Ezra 5:1-2; Ezra 6:14). The book calls him "the LORD's messenger" (1:13) and repeats its formulas "the word of the LORD came," "the LORD declares" and "the LORD of Armies says this." A Jewish tradition counts him among the last prophets, after whom the Holy Spirit left Israel (Bavli Yoma 9b).

Haggai calls Zerubbabel "my servant" and says "I have chosen you," words the Bible uses of David (1 Kings 11:34; Psalm 78:70). Zerubbabel was a grandson of King Jehoiachin, whose line Jeremiah had said would not sit on David's throne (Jeremiah 22:24-30). He is not called king. The promise is the last statement in the book, and the sources do not say whether or how it was kept; Matthew 1:12-13 and Luke 3:27 place him in Jesus' ancestry.
sections.refs: Haggai 2:23; Jeremiah 22:24-30; 1 Kings 11:34; Psalm 78:70; Matthew 1:12-13; Luke 3:27

sections.h: Zerubbabel and "the desire of all nations"
sections.b: Two parts of Haggai have been read messianically. The promise to Zerubbabel as a seal ring (2:23) was read as a hope for the Davidic ruler, and later as a type of Christ. The Hebrew phrase for the desire of all nations (2:7) became in the Vulgate "the Desired of all nations," a title of Christ; the Hebrew grammar favors "the prized things of all the nations." Both are receptions of the text, not translations of it, and the churches differ (see the cards).

sections.h: After the return: the stalled Temple
sections.b: Haggai belongs to the return from exile, not the exile itself. The community is back in Judah, 18 years after Cyrus's decree and 66 years after the Temple's burning, and the book shows the return as slow, poor and disappointed. The first-glory people (2:3) are those who remember 586 BC. The book's answer is not a new return but a present obedience.

Haggai builds the house Cyrus's decree allowed, not the temple of Ezekiel 40-48. The sixty-cubit house of Ezra 6:3 has none of the vision's dimensions or arrangements. Haggai's promise that the glory will fill the house (2:7, 9) echoes Ezekiel 43:1-5, where the glory returns to the new temple. How the two relate is debated: as a partial fulfillment, as a deferred hope, or, for Dispensationalists, as a future temple.

sections.h: Zerubbabel as the LORD's seal ring
sections.b: Haggai 2:23 reverses Jeremiah 22:24-25: the LORD had said he would pull Coniah (Jehoiachin) off his hand like a seal ring; now he takes Coniah's grandson and makes him one, "for I have chosen you." Sirach 49:11-12 praises Zerubbabel in the same image.

Haggai has the LORD say twice that he is about to shake the heavens and the earth (2:6, 21). The first brings the nations' wealth to the house (2:7-8); the second overturns the thrones and armies of the nations (2:22) and ends with the seal ring for Zerubbabel. Hebrews 12:26-27 quotes the first in the Greek form.

sections.h: The people of the land in Haggai
sections.b: Haggai calls on "all you people of the land" to be strong and work (2:4), alongside Zerubbabel and Joshua. Here the phrase is positive and probably names the Judean community as a whole; in Ezra 4:4 the same words name those who opposed the Temple.

sections.h: Haggai 2:7 in the Hebrew, the Greek and the Vulgate
sections.b: The Hebrew has a singular noun "desire" and a plural verb "will come"; the Septuagint has "the chosen things of all the nations will come"; the Vulgate has "the Desired of all nations will come." The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew with "the prized things of all the nations."

sections.h: Dew, drought and the unsown seed (Haggai)
sections.b: Haggai sets the grain, the new wine and the fresh oil (1:11) beside the vine, the fig, the pomegranate and the olive (2:19). The harvests failed in the years before; from the day the foundation is set the LORD promises blessing before any crop has come. Half the grain and two fifths of the wine (2:16) show the scale of the loss.

sections.h: The seventh day of Booths in Haggai
sections.b: Haggai's second message comes on the twenty-first day of the seventh month, the seventh day of Booths, 17 October 520 BC (2:1). Solomon dedicated his Temple at this feast (1 Kings 8:2), and Ezra says the returnees kept it when they set up the altar (Ezra 3:4). The date suits a message comparing the new house with the old.

sections.h: An excuse about the seventy years?
sections.b: Some commentators think the people's "The time has not come" (1:2) meant that the seventy years of Jeremiah 25:11-12 and 29:10 were not complete: counted from 586 BC they end in 516. Haggai does not mention the point, and the Temple was finished in 515.

In Haggai the LORD rouses the spirit of the governor, the high priest and the remnant (1:14), and says his spirit "is standing among" them (2:5). Zechariah in the same years says the work is done "Not by strength and not by force, but by my Spirit" (Zechariah 4:6). A Jewish tradition counts the Holy Spirit among five things the Second Temple lacked (Yoma 21b); Haggai's words are the other side of that teaching.

Haggai and Zechariah prophesied in the same months of 520 BC and Ezra names them together (Ezra 5:1; Ezra 6:14). Zechariah's first message comes in the eighth month, between Haggai's second and third (Zechariah 1:1), and his night visions in the eleventh month (Zechariah 1:7). Both name Zerubbabel and Joshua, and Zechariah 8:9-12 repeats Haggai's promise of blessing.

sections.b: Haggai is tenth of the Twelve in both the Hebrew and Greek orders, placed after Zephaniah and before Zechariah. It and Zechariah 1-8 share dates by Darius's year, month and day, and some scholars think they were edited together (Nogalski, Redditt). Its own place in the Twelve's story is the Temple's rebuilding after the exile.

Haggai 2:23 reverses Jeremiah's word about King Jehoiachin (Coniah): the LORD would pull him off like a seal ring (Jeremiah 22:24). Zerubbabel, his grandson through Shealtiel, is the one chosen. The Chronicler's list gives Shealtiel as Jehoiachin's son (1 Chronicles 3:17).

Haggai names finished houses and a bag with holes (1:4, 6) and sets them against the LORD's claim: "The silver belongs to me, and the gold belongs to me" (2:8). The book neither condemns wealth nor promises it. It asks where the effort goes.
